claim: Ankyrins are a family of scaffold proteins which play essential roles in connecting numerous ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and receptors to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton beneath membranes.
source: Ankyrins are a family of scaffold proteins which play essential roles in connecting numerous ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and receptors to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton beneath membranes and thereby provide mechanical support for plasma membranes and control the activities of excitable tissues including neurons and muscles (Bennett and Chen, 2001; Bennett and Healy, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Chen, 2001 and Bennett and Healy, 2009.

claim: There are three members in the human ankyrin family: ankyrin-R/B/G (AnkR/B/G) encoded by ANK1/2/3, respectively.
source: There are three members in the human ankyrin family: ankyrin-R/B/G (AnkR/B/G) encoded by ANK1/2/3, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of fact about the composition of the human ankyrin family, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: All three ankyrins consist of a highly similar N-terminal membrane binding domain composed of 24 ankyrin (ANK) repeats, a spectrin-binding domain comprised of two ZU5 domains, and a UPA domain followed by a death domain (DD) and a variable C-terminal regulatory domain.
source: They all consist of a highly similar N-terminal membrane binding domain composed of 24 ankyrin (ANK) repeats, a spectrin-binding domain comprised of two ZU5 domains, and a UPA domain followed by a death domain (DD) and a variable C-terminal regulatory domain (Bennett and Lorenzo, 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bennett and Lorenzo, 2013, and by Figure 1A showing the domain organization.

claim: The three ankyrins have distinct and non-overlapping functions in specific membrane domains coordinated by ankyrin-spectrin networks.
source: Although sharing similar domain organization, the three ankyrins have distinct and non-overlapping functions in specific membrane domains coordinated by ankyrin-spectrin networks (Mohler et al., 2002; Abdi et al., 2006; He et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohler et al., 2002; Abdi et al., 2006; He et al., 2013.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ankyrins can cause hemolytic anemia.
source: For example, loss-of-function mutations can cause hemolytic anemia (Gallagher, 2005), various cardiac diseases including several cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003, 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorder (Ferreira et al., 2008; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), and autism spectrum disorder (Iqbal et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gallagher, 2005.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ankyrins can cause various cardiac diseases including several cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction.
source: For example, loss-of-function mutations can cause hemolytic anemia (Gallagher, 2005), various cardiac diseases including several cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003, 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorder (Ferreira et al., 2008; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), and autism spectrum disorder (Iqbal et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohler et al., 2003, 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ankyrins can cause bipolar disorder.
source: For example, loss-of-function mutations can cause hemolytic anemia (Gallagher, 2005), various cardiac diseases including several cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003, 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorder (Ferreira et al., 2008; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), and autism spectrum disorder (Iqbal et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferreira et al., 2008; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ankyrins can cause autism spectrum disorder.
source: For example, loss-of-function mutations can cause hemolytic anemia (Gallagher, 2005), various cardiac diseases including several cardiac arrhythmia syndromes and sinus node dysfunction (Mohler et al., 2003, 2007; Le Scouarnec et al., 2008; Hashemi et al., 2009), bipolar disorder (Ferreira et al., 2008; Dedman et al., 2012; Rueckert et al., 2013), and autism spectrum disorder (Iqbal et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Iqbal et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Ankyrins bind to and anchor numerous membrane targets via their N-terminal 24 ANK repeats to specific membrane micro-domains in coordination with spectrin-based cytoskeletal structures.
source: The wide-ranging physiological functions of ankyrins are the result of ankyrin's remarkable capacity for binding to and anchoring numerous membrane targets, via their N-terminal 24 ANK repeats, to specific membrane micro-domains in coordination with spectrin-based cytoskeletal structures (Bennett and Chen, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bennett and Chen, 2001.

claim: Interaction between AnkG and L1 cell adhesion molecules (e.g., the 186 kDa neurofascin) is required for the formation and stability of the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: Interaction between AnkG and L1 cell adhesion molecules (e.g., the 186 kDa neurofascin, referred to as Nfasc in this study) is required for the formation and stability of the AIS (Hedstrom et al., 2007; Zonta et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hedstrom et al., 2007; Zonta et al., 2011.

claim: AnkG is responsible for clustering voltage-gated sodium channels at the AIS, which underlies the mechanistic basis of action potential generation and propagation.
source: AnkG is in turn responsible for clustering voltage-gated sodium channels at the AIS, which underlies the mechanistic basis of action potential generation and propagation (Garrido et al., 2003; Kole et al., 2008) (see review by Rasband, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garrido et al., 2003; Kole et al., 2008 and a review by Rasband, 2010.

claim: Anchoring of L1 cell adhesion molecules directs inhibitory GABAergic synapse innervation at the AIS of excitatory Purkinje neurons.
source: Anchoring of L1 cell adhesion molecules also directs inhibitory GABAergic synapse innervation at the AIS of excitatory Purkinje neurons (Ango et al., 2004), a critical step for balanced neuronal circuit formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ango et al., 2004.

claim: Depletion of AnkG both in cultured hippocampal neurons and in mice causes axons to lose axonal properties and acquire the molecular characteristics of dendrites.
source: Depletion of AnkG both in cultured hippocampal neurons and in mice causes axons to lose axonal properties and acquire the molecular characteristics of dendrites, showing that AnkG is required for the maintenance of axonal polarity (Hedstrom et al., 2008; Sobotzik et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hedstrom et al., 2008; Sobotzik et al., 2009.

claim: AnkG is required for the maintenance of axonal polarity.
source: Depletion of AnkG both in cultured hippocampal neurons and in mice causes axons to lose axonal properties and acquire the molecular characteristics of dendrites, showing that AnkG is required for the maintenance of axonal polarity (Hedstrom et al., 2008; Sobotzik et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hedstrom et al., 2008; Sobotzik et al., 2009.

claim: AnkB/G mediates coordination of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na/K ATPase, Na/Ca exchanger, and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptors in cardiomyocytes.
source: Other examples of ankyrin function in organizing membrane signaling networks include, but are not limit to, AnkB/G-mediated coordination of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na/K ATPase, Na/Ca exchanger, and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptors in cardiomyocytes (Mohler et al., 2004, 2005; Hund et al., 2008; Lowe et al., 2008) and the dystrophin/dystroglycan complex in skeletal muscles (Ayalon et al., 2008, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mohler et al., 2004, 2005; Hund et al., 2008; Lowe et al., 2008.

claim: Ankyrins mediate coordination of the dystrophin/dystroglycan complex in skeletal muscles.
source: Other examples of ankyrin function in organizing membrane signaling networks include, but are not limit to, AnkB/G-mediated coordination of voltage-gated sodium channels, Na/K ATPase, Na/Ca exchanger, and inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate receptors in cardiomyocytes (Mohler et al., 2004, 2005; Hund et al., 2008; Lowe et al., 2008) and the dystrophin/dystroglycan complex in skeletal muscles (Ayalon et al., 2008, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ayalon et al., 2008, 2011.

claim: AnkR is essential for preserving erythrocyte membrane integrity.
source: Finally, as originally discovered by Bennett and Stenbuck (1979a, 1979b), AnkR is well known to be essential for preserving erythrocyte membrane integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Stenbuck (1979a, 1979b).

claim: The C-terminal regulatory domain of AnkR binds to ANK repeats intra-molecularly and modulates the target binding properties of ankyrins.
source: The C-terminal regulatory domains have been reported to bind to ANK repeats intra-molecularly and modulate the target binding properties of ankyrins (Davis et al., 1992; Abdi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 1992; Abdi et al., 2006.

claim: AnkR_repeats interact with the entire C-terminal regulatory domain (residues 1529–1907) with a Kd of around 1 µM.
source: We measured the interaction of AnkR_repeats with its entire C-terminal regulatory domain (residues 1529–1907) using highly purified recombinant proteins, and found that they interact with each other with a Kd of around 1 µM (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A 48-residue auto-inhibitory segment (residues 1577–1624) is the complete ANK repeat-binding region in AnkR.
source: Using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)-based quantitative binding assays, we identified a 48-residue auto-inhibitory segment (residues 1577–1624, referred to as 'AS') as the complete ANK repeat-binding region (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC-based experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Further truncation at either end of the 48-residue AS fragment significantly decreased its binding to AnkR_repeats.
source: Further truncation at either end of this 48-residue AS fragment significantly decreased its binding to AnkR_repeats (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The auto-inhibitory segment (AS) is specific to AnkR and does not exist in AnkB or AnkG.
source: The corresponding sequence does not exist in AnkB or AnkG, indicating the AS is specific to AnkR (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AnkR_AS binds to AnkR/B/G ANK repeats with comparable affinities.
source: AnkR_AS was found to bind to AnkR/B/G ANK repeats with comparable affinities (Figure 1D), as expected since AnkR/B/G share extremely conserved ANK repeat sequences (Figure 2B and see below).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and sequence conservation data in Figure 2B.

claim: The structure of the AnkR_AS/AnkB_repeats fusion protein was solved at 3.5 Å resolution.
source: After extensive trials of screening and optimization, we succeeded in obtaining good-diffraction crystals of AnkR_AS fused at its C-terminus with the AnkB_repeats and solved the structure of the fusion protein at 3.5 Å resolution (Figure 2C and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: The NMR spectra of the 13CH3-Met selectively labeled fusion protein and the ANK repeats/AS complex produced by cleavage of the fusion protein at the fusion site are essentially identical.
source: The NMR spectra of the 13CH3-Met selectively labeled fusion protein and the ANK repeats/AS complex produced by cleavage of the fusion protein at the fusion site are essentially identical (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the fusion strategy used here facilitates crystallization but does not alter the structure of the ANK repeats/AS complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fusion strategy used facilitates crystallization but does not alter the structure of the ANK repeats/AS complex.
source: The NMR spectra of the 13CH3-Met selectively labeled fusion protein and the ANK repeats/AS complex produced by cleavage of the fusion protein at the fusion site are essentially identical (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the fusion strategy used here facilitates crystallization but does not alter the structure of the ANK repeats/AS complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the NMR data showing identical spectra in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are three Met residues in AS (Met1601, Met1604, and Met1607) and all three Met residues are in the binding interface between ANK repeats and AS.
source: There are three Met residues in AS (Met1601, Met1604, and Met1607) and all three Met residues are in the binding interface between ANK repeats and AS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The 24 ANK repeats form a left-handed helical solenoid with each repeat rotating anti-clockwise by ∼16°.
source: The 24 ANK repeats form a left-handed helical solenoid with each repeat rotating anti-clockwise by ∼16° (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Each ANK repeat has the typical ANK repeat sequence pattern and forms a helix-turn-helix conformation, except for the capping helices in the first and last repeats.
source: Except for the capping helices in the first and last repeats (i.e., αA of R1 and αB of R24), each repeat has the typical ANK repeat sequence pattern and forms a helix-turn-helix conformation (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: A well-defined finger-like hairpin loop (finger loop) connects two consecutive ANK repeats.
source: A well-defined finger-like hairpin loop (finger loop) connects two consecutive repeats.
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations from the crystal structure.

claim: The inner αA helices and the finger loops of the 24 repeats line together to form an elongated concave inner groove.
source: The inner αA helices and the finger loops of the 24 repeats line together to form an elongated concave inner groove, and the αB helices of the repeats form the solvent-exposed convex outer surface.
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations from the crystal structure.

claim: The ANK repeats superhelix has outer and inner diameters of approximately 60 Å and 45 Å, respectively, and a total height of ∼150 Å.
source: The ANK repeats superhelix has outer and inner diameters of approximately 60 Å and 45 Å, respectively, and a total height of ∼150 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The size of the ANK repeats revealed in the structure is consistent with previous measurement by atomic force microscopy.
source: The size of the ANK repeats revealed here is consistent with the previous measurement by atomic force microscopy (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with data from Lee et al., 2006.

claim: The C-terminal half of the ANK repeats structure aligns well with the apo-form structure of the last 12 ANK repeats of AnkR with an overall r.m.s.d. of 1.6 Å.
source: The C-terminal half of the ANK repeats structure aligns well with the apo-form structure of the last 12 ANK repeats of AnkR with an overall r.m.s.d. of 1.6 Å (Michaely et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison with data from Michaely et al., 2002.

claim: Conservation is above 80% at most positions of vertebrate AnkR/B/G ANK repeats.
source: We analyzed the amino acid residues at each position of vertebrate AnkR/B/G ANK repeats and found that conservation is above 80% at most of the positions (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Residues forming the target binding concave inner groove are essentially identical among vertebrate AnkR/B/G.
source: Further analysis reveals that residues forming the target binding concave inner groove (i.e., residues of the finger loops and αA helices of the 24 repeats) are essentially identical among vertebrate AnkR/B/G (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that both the structure and the target binding properties of their ANK repeats are likely to be the same (also see Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The structure and the target binding properties of ANK repeats are likely to be the same among vertebrate AnkR/B/G.
source: Further analysis reveals that residues forming the target binding concave inner groove (i.e., residues of the finger loops and αA helices of the 24 repeats) are essentially identical among vertebrate AnkR/B/G (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3), indicating that both the structure and the target binding properties of their ANK repeats are likely to be the same (also see Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from sequence conservation data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, and binding data in Figure 1D.

claim: The residues in the entire inner groove of the ANK repeats superhelix are highly conserved for all ankyrins throughout evolution (from worm to human).
source: Additionally, the residues in the entire inner groove of the ANK repeats superhelix are highly conserved for all ankyrins throughout evolution (from worm to human) (Figure 2D and Video 1), suggesting that the functions of ANK repeats in different species of ankyrins are highly conserved during evolution and that the inner groove of ANK repeats is the general binding site for membrane-associated targets of ankyrins.
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: The functions of ANK repeats in different species of ankyrins are highly conserved during evolution.
source: Additionally, the residues in the entire inner groove of the ANK repeats superhelix are highly conserved for all ankyrins throughout evolution (from worm to human) (Figure 2D and Video 1), suggesting that the functions of ANK repeats in different species of ankyrins are highly conserved during evolution and that the inner groove of ANK repeats is the general binding site for membrane-associated targets of ankyrins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from conservation data shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: The inner groove of ANK repeats is the general binding site for membrane-associated targets of ankyrins.
source: Additionally, the residues in the entire inner groove of the ANK repeats superhelix are highly conserved for all ankyrins throughout evolution (from worm to human) (Figure 2D and Video 1), suggesting that the functions of ANK repeats in different species of ankyrins are highly conserved during evolution and that the inner groove of ANK repeats is the general binding site for membrane-associated targets of ankyrins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from conservation data shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: Binding of AS to AnkG_repeats prevents voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2 and Nfasc from binding to AnkG.
source: Consistent with this prediction, binding of AS to AnkG_repeats prevents voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2 and Nfasc from binding to AnkG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Before binding to ANK repeats, AS adopts a random coil structure.
source: Before binding to ANK repeats, AS adopts a random coil structure as indicated by its NMR spectrum (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: In the complex, AS adopts a highly extended structure binding to part of the inner groove formed by the N-terminal 14 ANK repeats (R1–14) with its chain orientation anti-parallel to that of ANK repeats.
source: In the complex, AS adopts a highly extended structure binding to part of the inner groove formed by the N-terminal 14 ANK repeats (R1–14) with its chain orientation anti-parallel to that of ANK repeats (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: A 10-residue segment of AS (residues 1592–1601) forms an α helix when bound to ANK repeats.
source: A 10-residue segment of AS (residues 1592–1601) forms an α helix when bound to ANK repeats (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The binding of AS to ANK repeats can be divided into three sites (sites 1, 2, and 3) formed by the repeats 2–6, 7–10, and 11–14, respectively.
source: The binding of AS to ANK repeats can be divided somewhat arbitrarily into three sites (sites 1, 2, and 3) formed by the repeats 2–6, 7–10, and 11–14, respectively (Figure 2C and Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3A–C.

claim: The interactions in site 1 are primarily charge–charge and hydrogen bonding in nature, although hydrophobic contacts also contribute to the binding.
source: The interactions in site 1 are primarily charge–charge and hydrogen bonding in nature, although hydrophobic contacts also contribute to the binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The interactions in site 2 are mediated both by hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions.
source: The interactions in site 2 are mediated both by hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions, while interactions in site 3 are mainly hydrophobic (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Interactions in site 3 are mainly hydrophobic.
source: The interactions in site 2 are mediated both by hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions, while interactions in site 3 are mainly hydrophobic (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The Kd of the binding of AnkG_repeats to the Nav1.2_ABD is 0.17 μΜ.
source: The Kd of the binding of AnkG_repeats to the Nav1.2_ABD (residues 1035–1129, comprising the majority of the cytoplasmic loop connecting transmembrane helices II and III, see below for details) and to the Nfasc_ABD (a 28-residue fragment in the cytoplasmic tail; Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and see Garver et al., 1997) is 0.17 and 0.21 μΜ, respectively (Figure 3E, upper panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Kd of the binding of AnkG_repeats to the Nfasc_ABD is 0.21 μΜ.
source: The Kd of the binding of AnkG_repeats to the Nav1.2_ABD (residues 1035–1129, comprising the majority of the cytoplasmic loop connecting transmembrane helices II and III, see below for details) and to the Nfasc_ABD (a 28-residue fragment in the cytoplasmic tail; Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and see Garver et al., 1997) is 0.17 and 0.21 μΜ, respectively (Figure 3E, upper panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Garver et al., 1997.

claim: Mutations in site 1 (Phe131 and Phe164 in R4 and R5) significantly decreased ANK repeat binding to Nav1.2, but had no impact on Nfasc binding.
source: The mutations in site 1 significantly decreased ANK repeat binding to Nav1.2, but had no impact on Nfasc binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutations in site 2 (Ile267 and Leu300 in R8 and R9) had minimal impact on Nav1.2 binding, but significantly weakened Nfasc binding.
source: Conversely, the mutations in site 2 had minimal impact on Nav1.2 binding, but significantly weakened Nfasc binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutations in site 3 (Leu366, Phe399, and Leu432 in R11, R12, and R13) weakened ANK repeat binding to both Nav1.2 and Nfasc.
source: The mutations in site 3 weakened ANK repeat binding to both targets (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Nav1.2 binds to sites 1 and 3 of ANK repeats.
source: The above results indicate that the two targets bind to ANK repeats with distinct modes, with Nav1.2 binding to sites 1 and 3 and Nfasc binding to sites 2 and 3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Nfasc binds to sites 2 and 3 of ANK repeats.
source: The above results indicate that the two targets bind to ANK repeats with distinct modes, with Nav1.2 binding to sites 1 and 3 and Nfasc binding to sites 2 and 3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mutations in sites 1 and 2 led to ∼20-fold decrease in AnkR_AS binding.
source: The mutations in sites 1 and 2 led to ∼20-fold decrease in AnkR_AS binding, while the site 3 mutation only caused an approximately threefold decrease in AnkR_AS binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The site 3 mutation only caused an approximately threefold decrease in AnkR_AS binding.
source: The mutations in sites 1 and 2 led to ∼20-fold decrease in AnkR_AS binding, while the site 3 mutation only caused an approximately threefold decrease in AnkR_AS binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: KCNQ2 mainly binds to sites 1 and 2 of ANK repeats.
source: Finally, we tested the binding of another two reported ankyrin targets, the KCNQ2 potassium channel (Pan et al., 2006) and the voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Cunha et al., 2011), to the ANK repeats and its mutants, and found that KCNQ2 mainly binds to sites 1 and 2, and Cav1.3 primarily relies on site 2 of ANK repeats (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4B and citations to Pan et al., 2006.

claim: Cav1.3 primarily relies on site 2 of ANK repeats.
source: Finally, we tested the binding of another two reported ankyrin targets, the KCNQ2 potassium channel (Pan et al., 2006) and the voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Cunha et al., 2011), to the ANK repeats and its mutants, and found that KCNQ2 mainly binds to sites 1 and 2, and Cav1.3 primarily relies on site 2 of ANK repeats (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4C and citations to Cunha et al., 2011.

claim: Through combinations of multiple binding sites on the extremely conserved and elongated inner groove formed by the 24 ANK repeats, ankyrins can bind to numerous targets with diverse amino acid sequences.
source: Taken together, the above biochemical analysis plus the structure of the ANK repeats/AS complex reveals that through combinations of multiple binding sites on the extremely conserved and elongated inner groove formed by the 24 ANK repeats, ankyrins can bind to numerous targets with diverse amino acid sequences.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural and biochemical data presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: The intracellular loop connecting the transmembrane helices II and III (loop 2) is responsible for targeting Nav1.2 to the AIS via directly binding to AnkG.
source: Previous studies have reported that the intracellular loop connecting the transmembrane helices II and III (loop 2) is responsible for targeting Nav1.2 to the AIS via directly binding to AnkG, and identified a 27-residue motif within loop 2 ('ABD-C', indicated in Figure 5A,D) as the AnkG binding domain (Garrido et al., 2003; Lemaillet et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garrido et al., 2003; Lemaillet et al., 2003.

claim: A 95-residue fragment (ABD, residues 1035–1129) is sufficient for binding to AnkG.
source: First, we confirmed that a 95-residue fragment (ABD, residues 1035–1129; Figure 5D) is sufficient for binding to AnkG (Figure 3E, upper left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The C-terminal part of the ABD (ABD-C) binds to ANK repeats with an affinity ∼15-fold weaker than the entire ABD.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the C-terminal part of the ABD (ABD-C, the 27-residue motif identified previously for ANK repeats binding) binds to ANK repeats with an affinity ∼15-fold weaker than the entire ABD, indicating that the ABD-C is not sufficient for binding to ANK repeats (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The N-terminal 68-residue fragment of loop 2 (ABD-N, residues 1035–1102) binds to ANK repeats with a Kd of ∼8 μΜ.
source: Consistent with this observation, the N-terminal 68-residue fragment of loop 2 (ABD-N, residues 1035–1102) also binds to ANK repeats, albeit with a relatively weak affinity (Kd of ∼8 μΜ; Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The ABD-C fragment binds to repeats 1–6 (R1–6) of ANK repeats with essentially the same affinity as to the entire 24 ANK repeats.
source: We further showed that the ABD-C fragment binds to repeats 1–6 (R1–6) of ANK repeats, as ABD-C binds to R1–6 and the entire 24 ANK repeats with essentially the same affinities (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The Nav1.2 peptide segment binds to ANK repeats in an anti-parallel manner.
source: These results also reveal that, like the AnkR_AS, the Nav1.2 peptide segment binds to ANK repeats in an anti-parallel manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the binding data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: ABD-C binds to site 1 and ABD-N binds to site 3 of ANK repeats.
source: Taken together, the biochemical data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 5 indicate that two distinct fragments of Nav1.2 loop 2, ABD-N and ABD-C, are responsible for binding to ANK repeats. The previously identified ABD-C binds to site 1 and ABD-N binds to site 3 of ANK repeats, and the interactions between the two sites are largely independent from each other energetically.
evidence: The claim is inferred from biochemical data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 5.

claim: The interactions between sites 1 and 3 are largely independent from each other energetically.
source: Taken together, the biochemical data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 5 indicate that two distinct fragments of Nav1.2 loop 2, ABD-N and ABD-C, are responsible for binding to ANK repeats. The previously identified ABD-C binds to site 1 and ABD-N binds to site 3 of ANK repeats, and the interactions between the two sites are largely independent from each other energetically.
evidence: The claim is inferred from biochemical data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 5.

claim: The sequences of ABD-C (the first half in particular) are much more conserved than those of ABD-N among Nav1 members.
source: We noted from the amino acid sequence alignment of the Nav1 members that the sequences of ABD-C (the first half in particular) are much more conserved than those of ABD-N (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The C-terminal less-conserved 10 residues of ABD-C are not essential for Nav1.2 to bind to ANK repeats.
source: Further mapping experiments showed that the C-terminal less-conserved 10 residues of ABD-C are not essential for Nav1.2 to bind to ANK repeats (Figure 5B, top two rows).
evidence: The claim is supported by mapping experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The entire ABD-N is required for the channel to bind to site 3 of ANK repeats.
source: Truncations at the either end of Nav1.2 ABD-N weakened its binding to ANK repeats (data not shown), indicating that the entire ABD-N is required for the channel to bind to site 3 of ANK repeats.
evidence: The claim is supported by truncation experiments.

claim: The structure of a fusion protein with the first nine ANK repeats of AnkB fused at the C-terminus of Nav1.2_ABD-C was determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: We verified this prediction by determining the structure of a fusion protein with the first nine ANK repeats of AnkB fused at the C-terminus of Nav1.2_ABD-C at 2.5 Å resolution (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1; the ANK repeats/the entire ABD complex crystals diffracted very poorly, presumably because of the flexible nature of the interaction between Nav1.2_ABD-N and site 3 of ANK repeats).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: The extended Nav1.2_ABD-C peptide interacts with the surface of the inner groove formed by the first five ANK repeats.
source: In the complex structure, the extended Nav1.2_ABD-C peptide interacts with the surface of the inner groove formed by the first five ANK repeats (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The hydrophobic residues of Nav1.2_ABD-C and AS occupy very similar positions on the hydrophobic groove formed by residues from ANK repeats R4 and R5.
source: In particular, the hydrophobic residues of Nav1.2_ABD-C and AS occupy very similar positions on the hydrophobic groove formed by residues from ANK repeats R4 and R5, and subtle conformational differences in the finger loops of R4 and R5 can accommodate amino acid sequence differences between the two targets (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Subtle conformational differences in the finger loops of R4 and R5 can accommodate amino acid sequence differences between Nav1.2_ABD-C and AS.
source: In particular, the hydrophobic residues of Nav1.2_ABD-C and AS occupy very similar positions on the hydrophobic groove formed by residues from ANK repeats R4 and R5, and subtle conformational differences in the finger loops of R4 and R5 can accommodate amino acid sequence differences between the two targets (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The binding of ABD-C extends all the way to R1 via charge–charge and hydrogen-bond interactions.
source: Unique to Nav1.2, the binding of ABD-C extends all the way to R1 via charge–charge and hydrogen-bond interactions (Figure 6A,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A,E.

claim: Glu1112 of Nav1.2 occupies the identical position as Glu1622 of AS does in the ANK repeats/AS complex.
source: We noted that Glu1112, which is completely conserved in both Na+ and K+ channels and mutation of which in Nav1.5 to Lys is known to cause Brugada syndrome in humans (Mohler et al., 2004), occupies the identical position as Glu1622 of AS does in the ANK repeats/AS complex (Figure 3A and Figure 6A,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3A and Figure 6A,E.

claim: Glu1112 is completely conserved in both Na+ and K+ channels.
source: We noted that Glu1112, which is completely conserved in both Na+ and K+ channels and mutation of which in Nav1.5 to Lys is known to cause Brugada syndrome in humans (Mohler et al., 2004), occupies the identical position as Glu1622 of AS does in the ANK repeats/AS complex (Figure 3A and Figure 6A,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation data and citation to Mohler et al., 2004.

claim: Mutation of Glu1112 in Nav1.5 to Lys is known to cause Brugada syndrome in humans.
source: We noted that Glu1112, which is completely conserved in both Na+ and K+ channels and mutation of which in Nav1.5 to Lys is known to cause Brugada syndrome in humans (Mohler et al., 2004), occupies the identical position as Glu1622 of AS does in the ANK repeats/AS complex (Figure 3A and Figure 6A,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mohler et al., 2004.

claim: Glu1112 of Nav1.2 is buried deeply in the groove and forms hydrogen bonds with the sidechains of Thr94 and Asn98 in the R2 and R3 finger loop.
source: In contrast to the common expectation of directly interacting with positively charged residue(s), Glu1112 of Nav1.2 is buried deeply in the groove and forms hydrogen bonds with the sidechains of Thr94 and Asn98 in the R2 and R3 finger loop (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Glu1112 binding pocket formed by R2 and R3 is highly positive.
source: Charge potential calculation shows that the Glu1112 binding pocket formed by R2 and R3 is highly positive, and thus nicely accommodates the negatively charged carboxyl group of Glu1112 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by charge potential calculation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The charge reversal mutation of Nav1.2 (E1112K) abolished the channel's binding to ANK repeats.
source: As expected, the charge reversal mutation of Nav1.2 (E1112K) abolished the channel's binding to ANK repeats.
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: E1112Q- and E1112A-Nav1.2 mutations weakened the binding of Nav1.2 to ANK repeats by ∼30-fold.
source: Even mild substitutions (E1112Q- and E1112A-Nav1.2) weakened the binding of Nav1.2 to ANK repeats by ∼30-fold (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: E1112Q- and E1112A-Nav1.2 (or E1100 in Nav1.6) failed to cluster at the AIS of hippocampal neurons.
source: In agreement with our findings, E1112Q- and E1112A-Nav1.2 (or E1100 in Nav1.6) failed to cluster at the AIS of hippocampal neurons (Fache et al., 2004; Gasser et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fache et al., 2004; Gasser et al., 2012.

claim: Substitutions of Thr94 and Asn98 of ANK repeats with Ala and Glu, respectively, weakened the ANK repeats/Nav1.2_ABD interaction.
source: Conversely, substitutions of Thr94 and Asn98 of ANK repeats with Ala and Glu, respectively, also weakened the ANK repeats/Nav1.2_ABD interaction (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The 'FF' mutant of 270 kDa AnkG-GFP was concentrated normally at the AIS, but failed to rescue clustering of endogenous Nav at the AIS.
source: The 'FF' mutant of 270 kDa AnkG-GFP was concentrated normally at the AIS, but failed to rescue clustering of endogenous Nav at the AIS (Figure 7A,C,D), consistent with the significantly weakened binding of the mutant AnkG to Nav1.2 (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7A,C,D.

claim: The proper clustering of Nav at the AIS depends on AnkG.
source: The 'FF' mutant of 270 kDa AnkG-GFP was concentrated normally at the AIS, but failed to rescue clustering of endogenous Nav at the AIS (Figure 7A,C,D), consistent with the significantly weakened binding of the mutant AnkG to Nav1.2 (Figure 3E,F). This result confirms that the proper clustering of Nav at the AIS depends on AnkG (Zhou et al., 1998; Garrido et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7A,C,D and citations to Zhou et al., 1998; Garrido et al., 2003.

claim: Nfasc clustered properly at the AIS in neurons co-transfected with 'FF'-AnkG.
source: In contrast, Nfasc clustered properly at the AIS in neurons co-transfected with 'FF'-AnkG (Figure 7B,E), which was predicted since the 'FF' mutant had no impact on AnkG's binding to Nfasc.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7B,E.

claim: Both the 'IL' (site 2) and 'LF' (part of site 3) mutants of AnkG-GFP failed to cluster at the AIS of hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, both the 'IL' (site 2) and 'LF' (part of site 3) mutants of AnkG-GFP failed to cluster at the AIS of hippocampal neurons (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the L1-family members (Nfasc and/or Nr-CAM) or other potential ANK repeats site 2/3 binding targets may play a role in anchoring AnkG at the AIS.
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The L1-family members (Nfasc and/or Nr-CAM) or other potential ANK repeats site 2/3 binding targets may play a role in anchoring AnkG at the AIS.
source: Interestingly, both the 'IL' (site 2) and 'LF' (part of site 3) mutants of AnkG-GFP failed to cluster at the AIS of hippocampal neurons (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the L1-family members (Nfasc and/or Nr-CAM) or other potential ANK repeats site 2/3 binding targets may play a role in anchoring AnkG at the AIS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'IL' and 'LF' mutants cannot rescue the clustering defects of Nav or Nfasc caused by the knockdown of endogenous AnkG.
source: Not surprisingly, neither of these mutants can rescue the clustering defects of Nav or Nfasc caused by the knockdown of endogenous AnkG (Figure 7D,E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuronal imaging data shown in Figure 7D,E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins have remained essentially the same for at least 500 million years.
source: However, the N-terminal 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins have remained essentially the same for at least 500 million years (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The membrane targets for ankyrins have expanded greatly in respond to physiological needs throughout evolution.
source: In contrast, the membrane targets for ankyrins have expanded greatly in respond to physiological needs (e.g., fast signaling in neurons and heart muscles in mammals) throughout evolution, and these membrane targets almost invariably bind to the 24 ANK repeats of ankyrins.
evidence: The claim is based on evolutionary analysis and established knowledge.

claim: The 24 ANK repeats form an elongated, continuous solenoid structure with its extremely conserved target binding inner groove spanning a total length of ∼210 Å.
source: The 24 ANK repeats form an elongated, continuous solenoid structure with its extremely conserved target binding inner groove spanning a total length of ∼210 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Three distinct target binding sites were identified in the first 14 repeats.
source: We identified three distinct target binding sites in the first 14 repeats (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Three to five ANK repeats can form a stable structural unit capable of recognizing certain target sequences.
source: This is in agreement with earlier studies showing that three to five ANK repeats can form a stable structural unit capable of recognizing certain target sequences (Li et al., 2006; Tamaskovic et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2006; Tamaskovic et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012.

claim: The last 10 ANK repeats of ankyrins can contain an additional two to three target binding sites.
source: Therefore, we predict that the last 10 ANK repeats of ankyrins can contain an additional two to three target binding sites.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the structural analysis of the first 14 repeats.

claim: The target binding sites on ANK repeats behave rather independently.
source: Importantly, the target binding sites on ANK repeats behave rather independently, as mutations/disruptions of interactions in each site do not lead to large perturbations in the interactions in the neighboring sites (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ANK repeats targets bind to the inner groove with extended conformations.
source: Equal importantly, the ANK repeats targets bind to the inner groove with extended conformations, and the segments responsible for binding to each site do not seem to cooperate with each other (i.e., an alteration in one segment does not have a large impact on the neighboring segments) (Figure 3 and Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: The multiple target binding sites on ANK repeats are quasi-independent.
source: Therefore, the multiple target binding sites on ANK repeats are quasi-independent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural and biochemical data presented.

claim: Combinatorial usage of multiple quasi-independent sites can in principle generate a large repertoire of binding targets with different sequences for ANK repeats.
source: One can envision that such combinatorial usage of multiple quasi-independent sites can in principle generate a large repertoire of binding targets with different sequences for ANK repeats.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The combinatorial usage of the quasi-independent sites, together with the low sequence specificity of each binding site as well as the structural plasticity of the ANK repeat solenoid, indicate that ANK repeats can have large capacities in binding to numerous membrane targets with diverse sequences.
source: The combinatorial usage of the quasi-independent sites, together with the low sequence specificity of each binding site as well as the structural plasticity of the ANK repeat solenoid (Lee et al., 2006), indicate that ANK repeats can have large capacities in binding to numerous membrane targets with diverse sequences.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural and biochemical data and citation to Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Unidentified ANK repeat binding proteins will likely be difficult to predict simply based on amino acid sequences.
source: In light of the above points, unidentified ANK repeat binding proteins will likely be difficult to predict simply based on amino acid sequences, although a firm conclusion awaits detailed characterizations of more ankyrin binding targets.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the findings presented.

claim: Combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has been observed in other long repeat-containing proteins including the Karyopherin family nuclear import/export scaffold proteins.
source: The combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has also been observed in other long repeat-containing proteins including the Karyopherin family nuclear import/export scaffold proteins (Conti et al., 1998; Kobe, 1999; Chook and Blobel, 2001; Xu et al., 2010), the Wnt signaling regulatory scaffold β-catenin (Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001), and tetratricopeptide repeats protein LGN/Pins (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Conti et al., 1998; Kobe, 1999; Chook and Blobel, 2001; Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has been observed in the Wnt signaling regulatory scaffold β-catenin.
source: The combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has also been observed in other long repeat-containing proteins including the Karyopherin family nuclear import/export scaffold proteins (Conti et al., 1998; Kobe, 1999; Chook and Blobel, 2001; Xu et al., 2010), the Wnt signaling regulatory scaffold β-catenin (Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001), and tetratricopeptide repeats protein LGN/Pins (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001.

claim: Combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has been observed in tetratricopeptide repeats protein LGN/Pins.
source: The combinatorial usage of multiple binding sites has also been observed in other long repeat-containing proteins including the Karyopherin family nuclear import/export scaffold proteins (Conti et al., 1998; Kobe, 1999; Chook and Blobel, 2001; Xu et al., 2010), the Wnt signaling regulatory scaffold β-catenin (Graham et al., 2000; Huber and Weis, 2001), and tetratricopeptide repeats protein LGN/Pins (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2011.

claim: Such a combinatorial target binding strategy may be a common feature for many other elongated repeat-containing proteins in diverse living organisms.
source: It is possible such a combinatorial target binding strategy may be a common feature for many other elongated repeat-containing proteins in diverse living organisms.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the findings and comparisons with other proteins.
